FLASHCARD SET · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Animal Categories flashcards.

Twenty-three animal families, twenty-three spotter sheets, ninety-two labeled animals a kid can read. Each card gathers one family — the pets that share our houses, the farm crew that feeds us, the wild cats with their whiskers, the giants of the ocean — and each card page carries a simple guide: who belongs to the family, what the animals do, and one way to play the whole family at home tonight. The deck starts with the animals your child already loves and walks outward, family by family, until the whole animal kingdom sits on the floor in rows — and the dinosaurs of long ago now have a whole class of their own at /dinosaurs/.

Every card in the set.

Every card is right here on one page, and every card shows its age pill — start with the group that fits your child today.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    The Big Sort

    Lay all the cards face up and sort the whole zoo into teams: fur, feathers, scales, shells. Count each team out loud — which team won today? Sort again tomorrow by big and small, or by where they live.

  2. 02

    Four a side

    Every card is a two-by-two sheet of four animals. Pick one animal from each square and tell one true thing about it — "the duck swims, the goat climbs, the horse runs fast!" Ninety-two animals, one thing each.

  3. 03

    Spot the repeat visitor

    Some animals sneak onto two cards: the penguin flies with the birds AND slides with the arctic crew, the parrot sits with the birds AND the rainforest crew, the frog hops with the amphibians AND the rainforest. Find every double!

  4. 04

    Fur, feathers, scales, shells

    Hold a toy animal up against the wall of cards and ask: where does this friend belong? Sorting by body cover is the first real science a child does — and every card on the floor is an answer.

  5. 05

    One square a day

    Read one square of one card at breakfast — a twenty-second animal visit. At that pace the whole deck takes a month, and every animal gets its own morning.

      Pets Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 3+Pets & farm friends

      Pets are the animals that live in our houses and love us back: they eat from our hands, sleep in our rooms and learn our names. On the card, four famous pets sit in their squares — a dog, a cat, a rabbit and a hamster — every one a friend a family might have.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Pets! These are the animals that live at home with us. Dogs wag their tails, cats purr, rabbits hop, and hamsters run on their wheel all night. We feed them, we are gentle with them, and they are our friends.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play pet shop with the stuffed animals: one shopkeeper, one customer, and every pet needs a name, a favorite food and a home box. Being gentle is the rule of the whole game.

      Quick parent note

      A rabbit is a rabbit everywhere — and bunny is the affectionate word both US and UK families use. Pets are usually the first animals a child can name, which is exactly why this deck starts here.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Pets lesson on the Learning Path.

      Farm Animals Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 3+Pets & farm friends

      Farm animals are the crew that feeds the town: the cow gives milk, the pig is clever with its snout, the sheep grows wool for sweaters, and the horse carries work and riders alike. On the card, the barnyard’s famous four stand in their squares, each wearing its job.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Farm animals! The cow says moo and gives us milk, the pig says oink, the sheep says baa and gives us wool, and the horse says neigh and gives us rides. The farm is a whole team of helpers!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Old MacDonald with actions: one corner of the room is the barn, and every animal card sends a different animal walk — stomp like a horse, wiggle like a pig, nibble like a sheep. Sounds on, of course.

      Quick parent note

      Cows, pigs, sheep and horses look the same in every country of the world — a cow is a cow in the US, the UK and Canada. Visiting a farm or petting zoo turns this card into a real day out.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Farm Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      More Farm Animals Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 3+Pets & farm friends

      The barn has more than four doors: the goat climbs everything, the donkey carries loads and sings its loud hee-haw, the alpaca grows the softest wool in the barnyard, and the buffalo is the big quiet one in the back field. On the card, the second farm crew stands ready.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “More farm animals! The goat climbs, the donkey sings hee-haw, the alpaca wears fluffy wool like a sweater, and the buffalo is big and strong. Every barn has more friends than you think!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Farm-charades: act one animal at a time — climb like a goat, carry a cushion like a donkey, fluff like an alpaca, stomp like a buffalo — and the family guesses. The hee-haw always gives it away.

      Quick parent note

      Alpacas and buffalo are the barn’s special guests — many children meet them first on cards like this one. Ask which barn animal your child would pick as a neighbor, and why.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the More Farm Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      Farm Birds Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 3+Pets & farm friends

      The farm’s birds run the morning: the chicken lays the eggs, the duck paddles the pond, the turkey struts its tail feathers, and the goose honks like the farm’s own doorbell. On the card, all four stand in their squares — feathers, beaks and big opinions.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Farm birds! The chicken says cluck and lays eggs, the duck says quack and swims, the turkey struts — gobble gobble — and the goose honks louder than the tractor! Feathers and beaks everywhere.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Egg-carton march: line up four toy birds or paper cups as chicken, duck, turkey and goose, and walk each one its own walk — waddle, strut, paddle, honk. Feathers optional, noise not.

      Quick parent note

      Duck is both the bird and what it does — paddle like a duck. The turkey is the famous guest at Thanksgiving tables in the US and Canada, which makes this card a seasonal favorite.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Farm Birds lesson on the Learning Path.

      Insects Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 3+Little crawly creatures

      Insects are the six-legged crew that fills the summer: the butterfly that used to be a caterpillar, the bee that makes honey, the ladybug that eats garden pests, and the dragonfly that flies sideways and backwards. On the card, four famous insects sit in their squares with their wings and spots.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Insects! Six legs, little bodies, big jobs. The butterfly flies from flower to flower, the bee makes honey, the ladybug — some say ladybird — eats the bugs that bother plants, and the dragonfly zips over the pond like a tiny helicopter.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Bug walk: in the garden or the park, hunt for the four card insects with your eyes only — no touching needed. Count wings, count legs, and give every found bug a name of its own.

      Quick parent note

      American families say ladybug; British families say ladybird — same little red beetle with the black spots, and both names fit on this card. Insects have six legs: counting the legs on each square is the game.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Insects lesson on the Learning Path.

      Garden Creatures Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 3+Little crawly creatures

      The garden has workers nobody sees: the snail that carries its house, the earthworm that turns the soil, the caterpillar that will one day fly, and the grasshopper that jumps ten times its own length. On the card, the garden’s quiet crew waits in its squares.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Garden creatures! The snail carries its home on its back, the earthworm wiggles underground and helps the plants grow, the caterpillar munches leaves — munch, munch — and the grasshopper jumps! Jump, jump, jump!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      After the rain, go on a slow-creature hunt: snails and worms come out when the ground is wet. Watch how the snail leaves a shiny trail, then put every creature back where you found it.

      Quick parent note

      Worms are a garden’s best friends — they make tunnels that let air and water reach plant roots. A child who knows this will never squish one again. Slow looking is the whole skill on this card.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Garden Creatures lesson on the Learning Path.

      Small Animals Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 3+Little crawly creatures

      Big animals get the headlines, but small animals run the world: the mouse that squeezes through cracks, the guinea pig that squeaks for carrots, the mole that digs tunnels with shovel-hands, and the beaver that builds dams with its teeth. On the card, four small workers sit in their squares.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Small animals! The mouse is quick and quiet, the guinea pig squeaks wheek-wheek when it wants a snack, the mole digs tunnels under the grass, and the beaver builds houses out of sticks in the river. Small bodies, big work!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Small-animal obstacle course: crawl like a mouse, dig like a mole under a blanket, stack blocks like a beaver building a dam, and squeak like a guinea pig at the finish line.

      Quick parent note

      The beaver is nature’s engineer — its dams change whole rivers and create ponds where fish and frogs move in. The guinea pig is the card’s famous pet: it squeaks loudest when the fridge opens.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Small Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      Amphibians Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 4–5Little crawly creatures

      Amphibians live two lives, which is what their big name means: they start in the water as eggs and tadpoles, then grow legs and move onto land. On the card, the double-life crew sits in its squares — frog, toad, salamander and newt, all with smooth, damp skin.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Amphibians! They live in water AND on land — two homes, one animal. The frog hops and sings ribbit, the toad walks and warts, the salamander and the newt have tails and like the rain. Damp skin, big adventures!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Play the frog life cycle: crouch small as an egg, wiggle as a tadpole, sprout arms and legs, then HOP around the room as a frog. The metamorphosis dance is the lesson, and it ends in jumping.

      Quick parent note

      This is the set’s first big word — amphibian — and four-year-olds wear it proudly once they can say it. Frogs sing loudest after rain; a springtime pond walk with this card is a whole science lesson.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Amphibians lesson on the Learning Path.

      Birds Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 3+Feathers, fins & scales

      Birds are the feathered family, and the only animals that fly — though not all of them do! On the card, four show-stoppers sit in their squares: the parrot that talks, the penguin that swims instead of flying, the owl that stays up all night, and the flamingo that stands on one leg.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Birds! Feathers, beaks, two wings, two legs. The parrot copies your words, the penguin waddles and swims, the owl says who-who in the dark, and the flamingo stands on one leg — try it! One leg is harder than it looks.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Bird Olympics: stand on one leg like a flamingo (count to five), waddle like a penguin across the room, turn your head slowly like an owl, and repeat one word three times like a parrot. Award a feather for each event.

      Quick parent note

      The penguin is the card’s trickster: it is a bird that cannot fly — its wings work as flippers. It shows up again on the arctic card, which makes it the deck’s first repeat visitor. Feathers are the one thing every bird wears.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Birds lesson on the Learning Path.

      Fish Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 3+Feathers, fins & scales

      Fish are the swimmers: they breathe water through gills, steer with fins and wear scales like armor. On the card, four fish hold their squares — the salmon that swims up rivers, the goldfish in its bowl, the toothy piranha, and the whiskered catfish from the muddy bottom.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Fish! They swim, they have fins and they breathe water — real water-breathers. The salmon swims upstream to where it was born, the goldfish swims in circles at home, the piranha has tiny sharp teeth, and the catfish has whiskers like a cat!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Fish-y yoga: lie on your back, arms and legs up, and wiggle everything — the goldfish wiggle. Then fold your hands into a fin and glide around the room. Bubble sounds required.

      Quick parent note

      Fish never stop being surprising: goldfish can remember things for months, and some catfish use their whiskers to taste the water. The piranha’s scary teeth are real but it eats mostly seeds and fruit — a good myth to gently fix.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Fish lesson on the Learning Path.

      Sea Creatures Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 3+Feathers, fins & scales

      The sea is full of animals that are not fish at all: the seahorse whose daddy carries the babies, the starfish that can grow a lost arm back, the crab that walks sideways, and the jellyfish that pulses like an umbrella made of glass. On the card, four ocean treasures sit in their squares.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Sea creatures! The seahorse swims standing up, the starfish has arms and no face you can point to, the crab walks sideways — side, side, side — and the jellyfish floats like jelly. The ocean is full of surprises!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Ocean-movement game: scuttle sideways like a crab, float slowly like a jellyfish with arms dangling, balance on one spot like a seahorse holding seagrass, and stretch five arms like a starfish.

      Quick parent note

      A starfish is properly called a sea star, and it is not a fish at all — no gills, no fins, no scales. The crab’s sideways walk is real: its knees only bend that way. Ocean words are a child’s first science vocabulary.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Sea Creatures lesson on the Learning Path.

      Reptiles Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 4–5Feathers, fins & scales

      Reptiles are the scaly sunbathers: no fur, no feathers, just beautiful scales — and they warm up their bodies in the sun because their temperature runs on sunshine. On the card, four scaly characters wait: the snake with no legs at all, the crocodile with its mighty jaw, the chameleon that changes color, and the lizard that can drop its tail and grow it back.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Reptiles! Scales and sunshine. The snake slithers — ssss — with zero legs, the crocodile snaps its big jaw, the chameleon changes its color to match the day, and the lizard does push-ups on a warm rock.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Reptile charades: slither flat like a snake, chomp slow-motion like a crocodile, change your "color" by walking to different-colored cushions, and do three lizard push-ups on the rug.

      Quick parent note

      Reptiles bask to warm up and rest in shade to cool down — they are the sun’s helpers in staying the right temperature. The chameleon does not just camouflage: it also changes color to "talk" to other chameleons.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Reptiles lesson on the Learning Path.

      Big Animals Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 4–5Big & wild

      Some animals are simply enormous: the zebra in its painted pajamas, the rhinoceros with a horn on its nose, the hippopotamus that lives half in the water, and the gorilla, the strongest cousin in the whole forest. On the card, the heavyweights hold their squares — every one bigger than a car door.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Big animals! The zebra wears stripes — no two zebras have the same stripes, like fingerprints! The rhino has a horn on its nose, the hippo loves the water and opens its mouth WIDE, and the gorilla beats its chest — boom, boom!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Big-animal measuring: lie down next to the sofa and ask "which big animal am I longer or shorter than?" Stripes made of painter’s tape on a t-shirt make an instant zebra.

      Quick parent note

      Zebras’ stripes confuse biting flies, hippos make their own sunscreen (a pink oily goo), and a gorilla’s arms are longer than its legs. Big animals eat mostly plants — the biggest bodies run on grass and leaves.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Big Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      Safari Animals Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 3+Big & wild

      Safari is the Swahili word for journey, and this card is the journey’s greatest hits: the lion whose roar carries for miles, the elephant with a trunk that works like a hand, the giraffe with a neck taller than a doorway, and the monkey swinging through the middle of it all.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Safari animals! The lion is the king — ROAR — the elephant sprays water with its trunk, the giraffe eats leaves from the tops of the trees, and the monkey swings, swings, swings. Ready for the safari jeep?”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Safari drive: chairs in a row become the jeep, someone drives, and each animal card appears at a "window" — walk like an elephant with an arm-trunk, stretch high like a giraffe, prowl like a lion. Binoculars from toilet rolls complete the trip.

      Quick parent note

      An elephant’s trunk has about 40,000 muscles — it can pick up a single peanut or push over a tree. A giraffe’s neck has the same number of neck bones as you: seven, just much longer ones.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Safari Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      Wild Cats Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 4–5Big & wild

      Every house cat has wild cousins, and this card holds four of the famous ones: the tiger with its bold stripes, the leopard with rosette spots that carry its dinner up a tree, the cougar that prowls the Americas, and the lynx with its paintbrush ears. Big paws, whiskers, and very quiet feet.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Wild cats! The tiger is the biggest cat in the world — stripes, stripes, stripes. The leopard can climb trees carrying its dinner, the cougar purrs like a giant house cat, and the lynx has furry ears with little paintbrush tips!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Quiet-paws game: walk from couch to kitchen without making a single sound — cats land soft. Then one giant leap like a tiger, and a tree-climbing stretch like a leopard. Purring optional but encouraged.

      Quick parent note

      The cougar goes by three names: cougar, puma and mountain lion — all the same cat, and all three names are right. Tigers are the only big cats that like water; leopards are the champion tree-carriers of the cat world.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Wild Cats lesson on the Learning Path.

      Primates Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 4–5Big & wild

      Primates are the monkey-and-ape family — and your child’s family too, because people are primates as well. On the card, four cousins sit in their squares: the chimpanzee that uses sticks as tools, the orangutan with arms so long it hardly ever touches the ground, the baboon from the savanna, and the lemur with the ringed tail from Madagascar.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Primates! Our cousins with clever hands. The chimpanzee uses a stick to fish for termites, the orangutan hangs by its long arms, the baboon lives in big noisy troops, and the lemur waves its black-and-white ringed tail!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hand-skill minute: primates are famous for clever fingers — stack five small blocks, thread three big buttons on a string, turn three pages one at a time. Clever hands are the family superpower.

      Quick parent note

      A chimpanzee greeting its friend touches hands, hugs and kisses — a lot like us. Orangutans are the rainforest’s gardeners: they eat fruit, walk far, and plant the seeds wherever they wander, including on the rainforest card.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Primates lesson on the Learning Path.

      Forest Animals Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 4–5Where animals live

      Walk into the forest and you are inside somebody’s home: the bear that sleeps all winter, the fox with the white-tipped tail, the deer moving quietly between the trees, and the squirrel that hides acorns and finds most of them again. On the card, the forest crew stands between its squares.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Forest animals! The bear sleeps all winter — a very long nap! The fox has a white tail tip, the deer walks on quiet hooves, and the squirrel buries acorns — and remembers where, mostly!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Acorn hide-and-seek: hide five "acorns" (pebbles, balls of paper) around the room, then take turns being the squirrel who hunts them. The bear’s job is to sleep through the whole thing on the couch.

      Quick parent note

      Squirrels plant forests by accident: forgotten acorns grow into the next generation of trees. Bears’ winter nap is called torpor — not quite sleep, more like a very long doze with the alarm set for spring.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Forest Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · ANIMAL CATEGORIES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Desert Animals Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 4–5Where animals live

      The desert is the hottest, driest home in the world, and its animals are dressed exactly for it: the camel with its energy-packed humps, the meerkat that stands on guard duty, the scorpion that glows under UV light, and the fennec fox whose enormous ears work like air conditioners. On the card, the desert crew sits in its squares, cool as cucumbers.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Desert animals! The camel walks across the sand for days, the meerkat stands up tall to look for danger, the scorpion hides under rocks with its curly tail, and the fennec fox has the biggest ears in the desert!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Meerkat watch: one child stands on a cushion as the lookout while the others dig (in a sandpit or rice bin). Swap guards every ten seconds — real meerkat groups take turns on duty all day.

      Quick parent note

      A camel’s humps store fat, not water — the water tanks are its blood, which holds a huge amount. The fennec fox’s ears release body heat: built-in cooling, no electricity needed. Desert life is all clever tricks.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Desert Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · ANIMAL CATEGORIES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Arctic Animals Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 4–5Where animals live

      At the top of the world everything is white and blue, and the animals wear the thickest coats on Earth: the polar bear with fur that is actually hollow, the seal that naps on the ice, the penguin in its perfect tuxedo, and the walrus with two long tusks. On the card, the ice crew sits in its squares, warm as toast.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Arctic animals! It is cold, cold, cold — but not for them! The polar bear swims in icy water, the seal slides on its belly, the penguin waddles in its tuxedo, and the walrus has two big tusks for pulling out of the water. Brrr? Not for these friends!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Blubber experiment: put one hand in a bag of ice — brrr! Then put the same hand inside a second bag full of shortening (a "blubber glove") dipped in the ice, and feel how warm seals and penguins stay. Science, with wows.

      Quick parent note

      The penguin is a repeat visitor: it flew with the birds card and now lives here in its tuxedo. A polar bear’s fur looks white but each hair is hollow and clear — the sun does the painting. Penguin and polar bear never meet in the wild: penguins live at the South Pole, polar bears at the North.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Arctic Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · ANIMAL CATEGORIES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Australian Animals Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 4–5Where animals live

      Australia is an island with its own animal kingdom, and this card holds four famous citizens: the kangaroo that hops in giant leaps and carries its joey in a pouch, the koala that sleeps up to twenty hours a day in the eucalyptus tree, the wombat that digs with a cube-shaped... backside, and the platypus — a furry mammal with a duck bill that lays eggs.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Australian animals! The kangaroo hops — boing, boing — with a baby in its pouch, the koala naps in the tree all day, the wombat digs long tunnels, and the platypus has a duck’s bill and lays eggs! Australia is full of one-of-a-kind friends.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Kangaroo relay: jump from cushion to cushion with a stuffed toy tucked into a "pouch" (apron pocket, hoodie pouch). Dropping the joey sends you back one rock — Australia is big, take your time.

      Quick parent note

      Almost everything on this card is a marsupial — a mammal that carries its babies in a pouch — except the platypus, which is one of the only mammals on Earth that lays eggs. Wombats really do produce cube-shaped poop, and scientists spent years finding out why (it does not roll away).

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Australian Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · ANIMAL CATEGORIES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Whales & Dolphins Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 3+Giants & old wonders

      The ocean’s giants swim on this card — and every one of them breathes air like we do: the whale, the biggest animal alive today, the dolphin that whistles and plays, and the two gentle "sea cows", the manatee and the dugong, that graze the underwater meadows. Four squares, four friends, all coming up for air.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Whales and dolphins! The whale is bigger than a bus and sings songs across the whole ocean, the dolphin jumps and whistles hello, and the manatee and dugong are the sea’s gentle cows — they munch seagrass all day, slowly, slowly.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Whale-song phones: two paper cups joined by string, one person hums a long whale song, the other listens and answers. Then jump like a dolphin between the waves (two cushions) and float like a manatee on the rug.

      Quick parent note

      Whales and dolphins are mammals, not fish — they nurse their babies with milk and must come up to breathe, which is why they blow the famous spout. A manatee is sometimes called a sea cow; sailors once mistook dugongs for mermaids, which was generous of them.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Whales & Dolphins lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · ANIMAL CATEGORIES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Night Animals Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 4–5Giants & old wonders

      When the sun goes down, the night shift clocks in: the bat that sees with sound, the raccoon with its clever little hands, the hedgehog that rolls into a prickly ball, and the firefly that lights up the summer dark. On the card, the night crew sits in its squares, wide awake.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Night animals! While you sleep, they wake up. The bat flies in the dark using echoes — like shouting and listening for the bounce! The raccoon washes its food with clever fingers, the hedgehog curls into a ball, and the firefly blinks — blink, blink — to say good evening.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Flashlight fireflies: dim the lamps, give everyone a torch, and blink slow signals across the room — fireflies talk in blinks. Then wrap in a blanket and roll gently like a hedgehog ball (on a soft rug, one roll at a time).

      Quick parent note

      Bats are the only mammals that truly fly, and they find their way by echolocation — sound pictures. The hedgehog is a garden friend in British gardens; in North America the raccoon takes the night shift instead. A garden after dark is a whole second world.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Night Animals lesson on the Learning Path.

      FLASHCARD · ANIMAL CATEGORIES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

      Rainforest Animals Flashcard for Animals

      Ages 4–5Giants & old wonders

      The rainforest is the busiest home on Earth, and most of its life happens high in the trees: the parrot flashing its colors, the toucan with the banana-beak, the sloth that moves so slowly a whole garden of moss can grow on its fur, and the tree frog no bigger than a thumb. On the card, the treetop crew hangs in its squares.

      Download card ↓

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Rainforest animals! The parrot squawks in rainbow colors, the toucan has a beak as big as its body, the sloth moves in slow motion — slowwww — and the tree frog climbs the leaves with sticky toes. The rainforest is loud, green and full of life!”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Sloth speed race: the slowest animal wins! Crawl from chair to couch as slowly as possible without stopping — the last one to finish is the champion sloth. Then burst into five fast frog jumps to feel the difference.

      Quick parent note

      The parrot is a repeat visitor: it sat with the birds card and now hangs here. A sloth’s slow motion is its superpower — moving slowly means nobody notices it. Rainforests hold more kinds of animals than anywhere else on Earth, and half of them live in the treetops like this crew.

      Teach it, step by step
